screens.title: Introduction to Stream Processing and Azure Event Hubs
screens.narratorSegment: Stream processing is about acting on data the moment it appears, not waiting for periodic batches. In this chapter you will learn what continuous, unbounded streams are, why they enable low-latency insights, and how Azure Event Hubs serves as a scalable front door for ingesting those events. We will walk through core building blocks: namespaces, event hubs, partitions and partition keys, consumer groups, capture for archival, and throughput capacity. You will see practical scenarios where Event Hubs is the right choice — for example, ingesting thousands of IoT sensor readings per second for real-time monitoring and simultaneously archiving the same stream for later batch analysis. Along the way we’ll highlight common pitfalls such as hot partitions and overloading the default consumer group, and we’ll show concrete setup steps so you can provision a namespace and event hub safely. By the end you should understand how Event Hubs decouples producers and consumers, how partitioning enables parallelism while preserving order, and how capture simplifies long-term storage. Consider a monitoring pipeline: what immediate signal would you need to trigger an alert within seconds rather than hours?

Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Introduction

Introduction to Stream Processing

Real-time event ingestion with Azure Event Hubs

This lesson explores why processing unbounded streams as they arrive unlocks immediate reactions and low-latency insights. We introduce Event Hubs as the managed ingestion service that receives very high event volumes and decouples producers from consumers. Expect conceptual maps, practical configuration notes, and a short hands-on activity.

In this lesson
Understand stream processing, Event Hubs core components, partitioning and consumer groups, capture, and capacity planning.
Producers
Consumers
Storage
Coming up
A guided tour of Event Hubs architecture, hands-on setup steps, and best practices to avoid hot partitions and consumer group contention.
Visual concept
Producers send events
Event Hub receives and partitions
Multiple consumers read independently
Explore key topics
Stream processing: continuous analytics for immediate action.
Partitions: lanes that enable parallel reads while preserving local order.
Capture: automatic archival to blob or Data Lake without extra code.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why stream processing matters in modern systems, identify when Azure Event Hubs is the appropriate ingestion layer, describe Event Hubs architecture including namespaces and partitions, and understand how consumer groups and partition keys enable scale and ordering. Each objective pairs a conceptual understanding with a practical action. For example, you’ll know how to choose a partition key with high cardinality so events distribute evenly and avoid hot partitions; you will also be able to create a new consumer group to allow an independent application to read the full stream. These are not just labels — they are concrete skills you can apply when designing real-time pipelines for fraud detection, telemetry, or personalized UX. We will combine conceptual diagrams with step-by-step portal instructions so you can both reason about and implement Event Hubs correctly. As you progress, check your designs against common pitfalls like using a single consumer group for unrelated consumers or leaving partitioning decisions to chance.

screens.title: What is Stream Processing?
screens.narratorSegment: Stream processing means continuously analyzing and acting on data as it arrives, rather than waiting for periodic batch windows. This is different from batch processing, which groups data into finite datasets before analysis. A clear example is an online fraud detection system: transactions arrive one at a time and you want to flag suspicious ones immediately. Stream processing lets you compute rolling metrics, detect anomalies, and trigger actions in seconds or milliseconds. It also implies different design trade-offs: you need to manage event ordering, state across events, and fault-tolerant processing. One common misconception is that stream processing replaces batch processing entirely. In fact, many architectures use both: real-time paths for immediate reactions and batch paths for historical analysis. The chapter example includes a lambda-like pattern where Event Hubs feeds both a real-time consumer and a capture path to storage. When designing a streaming solution, ask what latency is acceptable, whether strict ordering is required, and how you will persist raw events for replay. These decisions shape partitioning, retention, and consumer group design. What is Stream Processing? means stream processing continuously analyzes events as they are produced, enabling immediate insights and actions while often coexisting with batch analysis.. In practical terms, continuous analysis of unbounded event streams. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Stream Processing
Definition

Continuous, low-latency analysis

Stream processing continuously analyzes unbounded streams such as transactions, telemetry, or click events. It is chosen where immediate reaction or low-latency insights are required.

Example: Fraud detection that flags suspicious transactions instantly.
Analogy: a live control room reacting to events as they happen.
Common misconception
Stream processing does not eliminate batch processing; many systems combine both for real-time and historical analysis.
Why it matters
Processing data as it arrives lets businesses react to incidents quickly, reduce data-to-decision time, and create personalized experiences based on recent events.
Design questions
  • Is ordering required for a set of events?
  • What latency is acceptable for actions?
  • Will you need to replay raw events?
Key takeaway
Stream processing complements batch paths and is chosen for immediate detection, low-latency metrics, and continuous analytics.
Check your understanding
Name a scenario where you must act within seconds and explain why stream processing fits.

screens.title: Why choose stream processing?
screens.narratorSegment: Stream processing is chosen when immediate insights or actions create business value. Typical drivers include low-latency detection, the need to react to individual events, and the capacity to handle large volumes produced at high velocity. For instance, an e-commerce platform may use streams to detect fraud patterns within seconds, or a manufacturing line may use sensor streams for predictive maintenance to avoid downtime. Without streaming, these systems would detect problems only after batch jobs complete, potentially missing critical moments. Stream processing also supports personalization: clickstreams analyzed in real time can tailor content to users during a session. However, streaming implies architectural trade-offs: you must plan for ordering constraints, state management, and at-least-once or exactly-once semantics depending on processing guarantees. It is common to pair streaming with archival storage so you retain raw events for later batch analysis, auditing, or replay. When evaluating whether to stream, ask which business questions require immediate answers, what latency threshold matters, and how reprocessing should be handled. Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Business Value
Why stream?
  1. Low-latency detection and reaction to events.
  2. Support for high-rate, continuous data such as IoT telemetry and clickstreams.
  3. Enables real-time personalization and monitoring.
Concrete example
A fleet of sensors sends telemetry each second; streaming allows immediate alerts for anomalies while older data is archived for trend analysis.
Trade-offs
  • Ordering guarantees can be harder to manage across partitions.
  • Stateful processing requires careful fault-tolerance and checkpoints.
  • Design must include replay and archival strategies for correctness and auditing.
Key takeaway
Stream processing is chosen for speed and immediacy; pair it with archival storage when you need both live reaction and later analysis.

screens.title: Azure Event Hubs overview
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Event Hubs is a managed data streaming platform that ingests large volumes of events and acts as the front door to event-driven architectures. Conceptually it decouples producers — devices or applications sending events — from consumers that process them. This decoupling improves resilience and scalability: producers don’t need to know about consumer topology, and consumers can operate at their own pace. Event Hubs provides a namespace as a management scope containing one or more event hubs. Each event hub organizes events into partitions to enable parallel consumption. Event Hubs is designed for high throughput and supports multiple consumers reading the same stream independently. It is often described as a message queue for big data because it focuses on throughput and parallel reads rather than single-consumer queuing semantics. Understanding this role helps you place Event Hubs in a pipeline: it is the ingestion layer that feeds real-time processors and archival storage without tight coupling between producers and downstream logic. In practical terms, a high-throughput event ingestion platform. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Event Hubs Overview
Core idea

Managed ingestion for big-data streams

Event Hubs receives millions of events per second, provides partitioning and consumer groups, and lets multiple applications read the same stream independently for real-time and batch needs.

Namespace: a container for one or more Event Hubs and their management settings.
Event Hub: an entity that receives and retains events, organized into partitions.
Consumers: multiple independent readers can process the same events without interfering.
Example pipeline
Producers send telemetry to Event Hubs. A real-time processor consumes events for alerting. Event Hubs Capture writes the same stream to Data Lake for historical analysis and replay.
Key takeaway
Treat Event Hubs as the scalable ingestion layer that keeps producers and consumers loosely coupled and supports multiple consumption patterns.

screens.title: Namespaces, Event Hubs, and Partitions
screens.narratorSegment: Event Hubs organizes its resources in a simple hierarchy. At the top is the namespace: a management scope that contains one or more event hubs and presents a unique fully qualified domain name. Within a namespace you create an Event Hub, which is the entity that receives and retains events. Each Event Hub subdivides its event stream into partitions, which are ordered sequences of events that can be read independently. Partitions enable parallelism: multiple consumers can read from different partitions concurrently, increasing throughput. When a producer sends an event it may include a partition key so events with the same key stay in the same partition and preserve relative ordering. If no key is supplied, events are distributed across partitions using round-robin. A frequent design decision is choosing the right partition count: too few partitions limit parallelism, too many can complicate consumer scaling. Plan partition count based on the expected parallelism of consumers and throughput units allocated to the namespace. Namespaces, Event Hubs, and Partitions means namespace → event hub → partitions. partitioning enables parallel reads while preserving local order when a partition key is used.. In practical terms, how event hubs structures and organizes events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Namespaces & Partitions
Hierarchy
Namespace: management scope and unique FQDN. Event Hub: the logical stream. Partitions: ordered sequences for parallel reads.
Partition count affects parallelism; choose based on expected consumer instances.
Partition key ensures related events stay in the same partition and preserve order.
If no partition key is provided, Event Hubs distributes events round-robin across partitions.
Concrete scenario
If you have four partitions and three instances of a consumer application, the platform will assign partitions so consumers share the load. Increasing partitions allows more parallel readers but requires planning for throughput and offset tracking.
Key takeaway
Partitioning is the primary scaling mechanism; choose keys and counts to distribute load evenly and preserve ordering where needed.

screens.title: Partition Keys and Hot Partitions
screens.narratorSegment: A partition key is a value supplied by the event producer that determines which partition receives an event. Using a partition key guarantees that all events with the same key go to the same partition, preserving their order relative to each other. This is essential when order matters for correctness — for example, processing events for a single user session or a device stream. However, a poor partition key choice can create hot partitions: if most events share the same key or the key has low cardinality, one partition will receive disproportionate traffic and become a bottleneck. A practical rule is to choose a key with high cardinality that evenly distributes events across partitions. One common misconception is that partitioning always ensures even distribution — it only does so when keys are well-chosen. When you cannot pick a high-cardinality key because ordering is required within a small set, plan for increased capacity on that partition path or shard the identifier so resulting keys distribute better. Partition Keys and Hot Partitions means use keys with high cardinality to spread load; use a key when ordering for a subset of events is required but watch out for hot partitions.. In practical terms, how keys affect ordering and load distribution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Partition Keys
How it works
When a producer sets a partition key, Event Hubs routes all events with that key to the same partition. This preserves order for related events.
Pitfall: hot partition
If a key has low cardinality, one partition receives most traffic and becomes a bottleneck.
Practical tips
  • Prefer high-cardinality keys for even distribution.
  • If order matters for only a small group, consider sharding the identifier to increase cardinality.
  • Monitor partition throughput to detect hotspots early.
Example
Device IDs with thousands of unique devices make good keys; a single account ID used by millions of events does not.

screens.title: Consumer Groups and Parallel Processing
screens.narratorSegment: A consumer group is a named view into an Event Hub's event stream. Each consumer group maintains its own offsets and allows a distinct application or purpose to read the full stream independently. This means two different applications can process the same events without interfering with each other. Within a consumer group, multiple instances of the same consuming application coordinate to share partitions: each instance will receive a subset of partitions so work is parallelized. For example, if AppA has three instances and AppB has two, create two consumer groups so each app reads all events independently. A common mistake is to use the default consumer group for multiple unrelated apps, which creates contention and complicates offset management. Another consideration is that the maximum parallelism for a consumer group is bounded by the number of partitions because each partition can only be read by one instance within the same consumer group at a time. Therefore plan partition count to match the desired parallelism of your consumer applications. Consumer Groups and Parallel Processing means use separate consumer groups for distinct applications; partition count limits parallelism within a consumer group.. In practical terms, how consumer groups enable independent reads and scale. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 6 › Chapter 6.1 › Consumer Groups
Role
A consumer group gives an independent cursor into the stream so multiple applications can each read all events without interfering.
Scenario
AppA (3 instances) and AppB (2 instances) should use separate consumer groups so each app gets the full stream and shares partitions within its group.
Scaling notes
  • Parallelism within a consumer group is limited by partition count.
  • Create a dedicated consumer group per independent application.
  • Monitor offsets and lag to ensure consumers keep up.
Key takeaway
Separate consumer groups for separate applications and size partitions to match per-group parallelism requirements.

screens.title: Event Hubs Capture
screens.narratorSegment: Event Hubs Capture is a feature that automatically writes events from an Event Hub to Azure Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage Gen2. This removes the need to implement a separate consumer just to archive raw events, simplifying architectures that need both real-time processing and long-term storage. Capture is useful for auditing, compliance, and batch analytics, and it supports a lambda-style pattern where a stream feeds both live processors and a persisted archive. When you enable capture, configure the capture window and destination container so files are written at a cadence that suits downstream batch jobs. A common misconception is that capture replaces the need for dedicated archival consumers in all cases; while capture simplifies many scenarios, you may still need custom consumers if you require different formats, enrichment pipelines, or immediate archival transformations. Capture is a low-effort way to ensure every event is retained outside Event Hubs for later analysis or replay. screens.title: Throughput Units / Processing Units
screens.narratorSegment: Throughput Units (TUs) or Processing Units (PUs) are the capacity constructs for Event Hubs that control maximum ingress and egress rates. You allocate units to ensure the namespace and event hubs can handle expected traffic volumes. While the chapter does not prescribe exact numbers, the key design point is to size capacity based on expected peak throughput and partition count. If you under-provision units, you may observe throttling under load. Conversely, over-provisioning increases cost without benefit. Monitor telemetry and scale units as traffic patterns change. Also remember partitions are the unit of parallelism, while throughput units are the throttling capacity. Together they shape how many events per second you can ingest and how many consumers you can support. Start with conservative units for testing and increase as you validate real traffic patterns. Keep an eye on hot partitions that can cause localized throttling even when overall capacity looks sufficient. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Best Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Designing with Event Hubs requires deliberate choices to avoid common mistakes. First, avoid using low-cardinality partition keys; they lead to hot partitions where a single partition receives most traffic. Second, don’t use the default consumer group for multiple independent applications. Create dedicated consumer groups so each application can maintain its own offset and processing logic. Third, plan partition count to match expected consumer parallelism because a consumer group’s parallelism is limited by partition count. Fourth, size throughput units conservatively and monitor for throttling, increasing units based on peak load tests. Finally, use Event Hubs Capture for automatic archival, but understand when a dedicated consumer is required for enrichment or format changes. Best practices include instrumenting partition-level metrics, validating key cardinality, and testing consumer scaling scenarios. These steps reduce surprises in production and ensure reliable, scalable ingestion. fullNarratorScript:
Stream processing is about acting on data the moment it appears, not waiting for periodic batches. In this chapter you will learn what continuous, unbounded streams are, why they enable low-latency insights, and how Azure Event Hubs serves as a scalable front door for ingesting those events. We will walk through core building blocks: namespaces, event hubs, partitions and partition keys, consumer groups, capture for archival, and throughput capacity. You will see practical scenarios where Event Hubs is the right choice — for example, ingesting thousands of IoT sensor readings per second for real-time monitoring and simultaneously archiving the same stream for later batch analysis. Along the way we’ll highlight common pitfalls such as hot partitions and overloading the default consumer group, and we’ll show concrete setup steps so you can provision a namespace and event hub safely. By the end you should understand how Event Hubs decouples producers and consumers, how partitioning enables parallelism while preserving order, and how capture simplifies long-term storage. Consider a monitoring pipeline: what immediate signal would you need to trigger an alert within seconds rather than hours?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain why stream processing matters in modern systems, identify when Azure Event Hubs is the appropriate ingestion layer, describe Event Hubs architecture including namespaces and partitions, and understand how consumer groups and partition keys enable scale and ordering. Each objective pairs a conceptual understanding with a practical action. For example, you’ll know how to choose a partition key with high cardinality so events distribute evenly and avoid hot partitions; you will also be able to create a new consumer group to allow an independent application to read the full stream. These are not just labels — they are concrete skills you can apply when designing real-time pipelines for fraud detection, telemetry, or personalized UX. We will combine conceptual diagrams with step-by-step portal instructions so you can both reason about and implement Event Hubs correctly. As you progress, check your designs against common pitfalls like using a single consumer group for unrelated consumers or leaving partitioning decisions to chance.

Beyond understanding terms, you will practice design decisions and implement a basic Event Hubs setup. Learn to pick partition counts based on parallel consumers, choose partition keys with high cardinality to avoid hotspots, and create dedicated consumer groups so independent applications can read the same stream without interference. You will also use Event Hubs Capture to archive raw events to blob or Data Lake for audit and batch analytics, which simplifies a lambda-style architecture. Throughout, we will point out common mistakes: using the default consumer group for everything, failing to plan partition counts, or selecting low-cardinality partition keys. Each objective includes a verified milestone so you can check your competency; the hands-on activity walks through creating a namespace and an event hub with four partitions and a consumer group for analytics. Apply these outcomes in a telemetry, fraud detection, or clickstream pipeline to measure latency gains and operational resilience.

Stream processing means continuously analyzing and acting on data as it arrives, rather than waiting for periodic batch windows. This is different from batch processing, which groups data into finite datasets before analysis. A clear example is an online fraud detection system: transactions arrive one at a time and you want to flag suspicious ones immediately. Stream processing lets you compute rolling metrics, detect anomalies, and trigger actions in seconds or milliseconds. It also implies different design trade-offs: you need to manage event ordering, state across events, and fault-tolerant processing. One common misconception is that stream processing replaces batch processing entirely. In fact, many architectures use both: real-time paths for immediate reactions and batch paths for historical analysis. The chapter example includes a lambda-like pattern where Event Hubs feeds both a real-time consumer and a capture path to storage. When designing a streaming solution, ask what latency is acceptable, whether strict ordering is required, and how you will persist raw events for replay. These decisions shape partitioning, retention, and consumer group design. What is Stream Processing? means stream processing continuously analyzes events as they are produced, enabling immediate insights and actions while often coexisting with batch analysis.. In practical terms, continuous analysis of unbounded event streams. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Stream processing is chosen when immediate insights or actions create business value. Typical drivers include low-latency detection, the need to react to individual events, and the capacity to handle large volumes produced at high velocity. For instance, an e-commerce platform may use streams to detect fraud patterns within seconds, or a manufacturing line may use sensor streams for predictive maintenance to avoid downtime. Without streaming, these systems would detect problems only after batch jobs complete, potentially missing critical moments. Stream processing also supports personalization: clickstreams analyzed in real time can tailor content to users during a session. However, streaming implies architectural trade-offs: you must plan for ordering constraints, state management, and at-least-once or exactly-once semantics depending on processing guarantees. It is common to pair streaming with archival storage so you retain raw events for later batch analysis, auditing, or replay. When evaluating whether to stream, ask which business questions require immediate answers, what latency threshold matters, and how reprocessing should be handled. Why choose stream processing? means choose streaming when immediate action or low-latency insights materially improve outcomes, and design for ordering and state needs.. In practical terms, drivers: low latency, immediate reactions, high velocity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Azure Event Hubs is a managed data streaming platform that ingests large volumes of events and acts as the front door to event-driven architectures. Conceptually it decouples producers — devices or applications sending events — from consumers that process them. This decoupling improves resilience and scalability: producers don’t need to know about consumer topology, and consumers can operate at their own pace. Event Hubs provides a namespace as a management scope containing one or more event hubs. Each event hub organizes events into partitions to enable parallel consumption. Event Hubs is designed for high throughput and supports multiple consumers reading the same stream independently. It is often described as a message queue for big data because it focuses on throughput and parallel reads rather than single-consumer queuing semantics. Understanding this role helps you place Event Hubs in a pipeline: it is the ingestion layer that feeds real-time processors and archival storage without tight coupling between producers and downstream logic. Azure Event Hubs overview means event hubs ingests high-volume events, decoupling producers from multiple independent consumers and enabling scalable real-time pipelines.. In practical terms, a high-throughput event ingestion platform. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Event Hubs organizes its resources in a simple hierarchy. At the top is the namespace: a management scope that contains one or more event hubs and presents a unique fully qualified domain name. Within a namespace you create an Event Hub, which is the entity that receives and retains events. Each Event Hub subdivides its event stream into partitions, which are ordered sequences of events that can be read independently. Partitions enable parallelism: multiple consumers can read from different partitions concurrently, increasing throughput. When a producer sends an event it may include a partition key so events with the same key stay in the same partition and preserve relative ordering. If no key is supplied, events are distributed across partitions using round-robin. A frequent design decision is choosing the right partition count: too few partitions limit parallelism, too many can complicate consumer scaling. Plan partition count based on the expected parallelism of consumers and throughput units allocated to the namespace. Namespaces, Event Hubs, and Partitions means namespace → event hub → partitions. partitioning enables parallel reads while preserving local order when a partition key is used.. In practical terms, how event hubs structures and organizes events. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A partition key is a value supplied by the event producer that determines which partition receives an event. Using a partition key guarantees that all events with the same key go to the same partition, preserving their order relative to each other. This is essential when order matters for correctness — for example, processing events for a single user session or a device stream. However, a poor partition key choice can create hot partitions: if most events share the same key or the key has low cardinality, one partition will receive disproportionate traffic and become a bottleneck. A practical rule is to choose a key with high cardinality that evenly distributes events across partitions. One common misconception is that partitioning always ensures even distribution — it only does so when keys are well-chosen. When you cannot pick a high-cardinality key because ordering is required within a small set, plan for increased capacity on that partition path or shard the identifier so resulting keys distribute better. Partition Keys and Hot Partitions means use keys with high cardinality to spread load; use a key when ordering for a subset of events is required but watch out for hot partitions.. In practical terms, how keys affect ordering and load distribution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A consumer group is a named view into an Event Hub's event stream. Each consumer group maintains its own offsets and allows a distinct application or purpose to read the full stream independently. This means two different applications can process the same events without interfering with each other. Within a consumer group, multiple instances of the same consuming application coordinate to share partitions: each instance will receive a subset of partitions so work is parallelized. For example, if AppA has three instances and AppB has two, create two consumer groups so each app reads all events independently. A common mistake is to use the default consumer group for multiple unrelated apps, which creates contention and complicates offset management. Another consideration is that the maximum parallelism for a consumer group is bounded by the number of partitions because each partition can only be read by one instance within the same consumer group at a time. Therefore plan partition count to match the desired parallelism of your consumer applications. Event Hubs Capture is a feature that automatically writes events from an Event Hub to Azure Blob Storage or Data Lake Storage Gen2. This removes the need to implement a separate consumer just to archive raw events, simplifying architectures that need both real-time processing and long-term storage. Capture is useful for auditing, compliance, and batch analytics, and it supports a lambda-style pattern where a stream feeds both live processors and a persisted archive. When you enable capture, configure the capture window and destination container so files are written at a cadence that suits downstream batch jobs. Throughput Units (TUs) or Processing Units (PUs) are the capacity constructs for Event Hubs that control maximum ingress and egress rates. You allocate units to ensure the namespace and event hubs can handle expected traffic volumes. While the chapter does not prescribe exact numbers, the key design point is to size capacity based on expected peak throughput and partition count. If you under-provision units, you may observe throttling under load. Conversely, over-provisioning increases cost without benefit. Monitor telemetry and scale units as traffic patterns change. Also remember partitions are the unit of parallelism, while throughput units are the throttling capacity. Together they shape how many events per second you can ingest and how many consumers you can support. Start with conservative units for testing and increase as you validate real traffic patterns. Keep an eye on hot partitions that can cause localized throttling even when overall capacity looks sufficient. Designing with Event Hubs requires deliberate choices to avoid common mistakes. First, avoid using low-cardinality partition keys; they lead to hot partitions where a single partition receives most traffic. Second, don’t use the default consumer group for multiple independent applications. Create dedicated consumer groups so each application can maintain its own offset and processing logic. Third, plan partition count to match expected consumer parallelism because a consumer group’s parallelism is limited by partition count. Fourth, size throughput units conservatively and monitor for throttling, increasing units based on peak load tests. Finally, use Event Hubs Capture for automatic archival, but understand when a dedicated consumer is required for enrichment or format changes. Best practices include instrumenting partition-level metrics, validating key cardinality, and testing consumer scaling scenarios. These steps reduce surprises in production and ensure reliable, scalable ingestion.
